cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Laughter – the sound of laughing when you are happy or hear something funny.

p.em: Example: Laughter is the best medicine for a sad day.

cosy-blockquote.p: Origin – the point where something begins or starts.

p.em: Example: Scientists are looking for the origin of human languages.

cosy-blockquote.p: Speech – the ability to speak or express thoughts with spoken words.

p.em: Example: His speech at the wedding was very beautiful and funny.

cosy-blockquote.p: Ape – a large animal with no tail that is closely related to humans (e.g. chimpanzee).

p.em: Example: The chimpanzee is a very smart ape that lives in Africa.

cosy-blockquote.p: Reveal – to show or make something known to others.

p.em: Example: These new facts reveal the secret of how birds migrate.

cosy-blockquote.p: Sound – something that you can hear.

p.em: Example: I love the sound of rain on my window at night.

cosy-blockquote.p: Play – to do activities for fun and enjoyment.

p.em: Example: The young puppies love to play in the green garden.

cosy-blockquote.p: Similar – looking or sounding almost the same as something else.

p.em: Example: Your new smartphone is very similar to mine.

cosy-blockquote.p: Tickle – to touch someone lightly to make them laugh.

p.em: Example: Children usually laugh a lot when you tickle their feet.

cosy-blockquote.p: Scientist – a person who studies or has expert knowledge of science.

p.em: Example: The scientist discovered a new species of plants in the forest.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
According to the article, why is laughter helpful when animals make friends?
★ What is something that always makes you laugh?

What is the basic start or origin of human words?
★ Do you prefer telling jokes or listening to stories?

How does chimpanzee speech sound different from our speech?
★ Have you ever laughed in a serious place?

How does a wild ape talk to other animals?
★ How do you show you are happy without words?

What do tests reveal about these animal sounds?
★ Do you think cats can laugh?

What is a funny play sound that you like?
★ How often do you laugh every day?

Why do young animals need to play together in the forest?
★ What is the funniest video you saw recently?

How is ape laughter similar to human laughter?
★ Is it easy for you to make people laugh?

What happens when you tickle a happy baby chimpanzee?
★ Who is the funniest person you know?

How does a scientist record sounds in the forest?
★ Do you think laughing keeps you healthy?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Will we build simple tools to check animal laughter?
★ Would you watch a robot comedy show?

Will we find the exact origin of humor in pets?
★ Would you be happy if plants had humor?

If animals learn human speech, how will we talk to them?
★ Can internet chatting replace real face-to-face talking?

Will humans protect every smart ape in the world?
★ What makes a story funny to everyone?

Will new tests reveal how brains understand jokes?
★ Does humor help you on busy days?

Can a forest sound help us know if animals are sick?
★ Should schools teach funny storytelling?

Will schools make play zones like chimpanzee homes?
★ Do you track your daily smiles?

Will we show that dogs make a similar sound when playing?
★ Do emojis replace real voices?

Why do monkeys tickle their friends to make alliances?
★ Do people laugh when they are scared?

Will every scientist work with animal translators?
★ Can you communicate with just laughs for a day?

ul.li: Incorrect: The chimpanzees is smart → Correct: Chimpanzees are smart ((Plural subject needs plural verb))
Incorrect: I am laugh a lot → Correct: I laugh a lot ((Simple present structure))
Incorrect: It depend of animal → Correct: It depends on the animal ((Depends + on, singular s))
